Unquenchable
un-kwench'a-bl
adj. (that cannot be put out; of the fire prepared for the impenitent)
From un- and quench, rendering the Greek asbestos — not extinguishable. The same root gives the mineral name; the point of the word is not heat but permanence.

Biblical Definition

John the Baptist preached it before Christ preached it: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12; and again Luke 3:17). The figure is a threshing floor at the end of harvest, where the winnowing fan separates what is kept from what is burned, and the separation is final. Our Lord uses the same term without softening it: better to enter into life maimed “than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched” (Mark 9:43). The Old Testament supplies the image He is drawing on, and it is the last verse of Isaiah: “their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24). Two things are asserted together in that line — the worm does not die and the fire is not put out — and both halves say the same thing about duration. The adjective is therefore doing precise doctrinal work. It does not describe how hot the fire is; it forecloses the hope that it will one day burn itself out, and with it forecloses annihilationism and universalism alike.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unquenchable as that cannot be quenched or extinguished, and applies it to fire and to thirst.

expand to see more

UNQUENCHABLE, a. That cannot be quenched or extinguished; inextinguishable; as unquenchable fire or flame.

2. That cannot be repressed or allayed; as unquenchable thirst.

QUENCH, v.t. To extinguish; to put out; as, to quench flame.

2. To still; to quiet; to repress; as, to quench a passion or emotion.

FAN, n. An instrument used for winnowing grain, by throwing it up and blowing away the chaff.

Key Scripture

Matthew 3:12 — "Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire."

Luke 3:17 — "Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable."

Mark 9:43 — "And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched:"

Isaiah 66:24 — "And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh."

Modern Corruption

The one adjective that forbids an end to the fire is explained away by the two doctrines that require one.

expand to see more

Annihilationism, sometimes called conditional immortality, argues that the fire is unquenchable only in the sense that nothing can interrupt it until it has consumed its fuel, after which the wicked cease to exist. The argument requires the word to mean the opposite of what it says. An unquenchable fire is one that cannot be put out; a fire that goes out when the fuel is gone has simply been quenched by exhaustion. Isaiah 66:24 blocks the reading twice over by pairing the fire with a worm that does not die — if the objects of judgment were consumed, the worm would starve. Evangelicals who have adopted this position in recent decades have not found a new exegesis; they have found the doctrine intolerable and adjusted the vocabulary.

Universalism takes the other road and makes the fire remedial — a purifying furnace from which all eventually emerge. This is Origen's error, condemned in the early church and revived in our own time under the euphemism of the larger hope. Neither Testament offers it. The fan separates wheat from chaff and the two go to different places; the chaff is not refined into wheat. The Confession states the biblical doctrine without flinching: the wicked shall be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction. It is not a doctrine any faithful man preaches with pleasure, and the Saviour who taught it more plainly than anyone else in Scripture wept over the city that would not come to Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek asbestos (G762), unquenchable — Matthew 3:12, Mark 9:43, Luke 3:17; Hebrew kabah, to be quenched — Isaiah 66:24.

expand to see more

Greek asbestos (G762) — not extinguishable; Matthew 3:12, Mark 9:43, Mark 9:45, Luke 3:17.

Greek ptuon (G4425) — the winnowing fan; Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17, its only occurrences.

Greek achuron (G892) — chaff; what the fan separates and the fire consumes.

Hebrew kabah — to be quenched or extinguished; Isaiah 66:24, negated, and Isaiah 42:3 of the smoking flax He will not quench.

Mark 9:48 repeats Isaiah 66:24 verbatim as the Lord's own commentary on the word.

Usage

"“He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” — the winnowing fan and a final separation."

"“Their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched” — both halves say duration."

"The word forbids the two escapes: it does not burn out, and it does not purify."
